attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡  Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡  Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: game set up, sprite set up, user input, game end.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use randint to randomize the sprite’s x and y-positions in the  setPosition code inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many times will the for loop run? How do you know?

❓ What happens when the for loop runs? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The default  expressions will begin the counter variable at 0 and run while the counter is less than 5. Since the increment increases the counter variable by 1 after each iteration, the loop, and the code inside of it, will run 5 times (0, 1, 2, 3, 4).

💡 Each time the for loop runs, a sprite will be set and placed randomly on the screen. Since the loop runs 5 times, 5 sprites will appear on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Use a for loop to add multiple sprites to the project!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath // sprite set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { }

The for loop has 3 expressions, separated by semicolons ;: initialization, run condition, and increment. Notice that the default initialization expression let i = 0 starts the counter at 0, the run condition i < 5 runs the code in the loop while the counter is less than 5, and the increment i++ increases the counter by 1 each time the loop runs. 


Add a sprite to appear on the screen 5 times. Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Select any sprite image and update the sprite name. 


Set the sprites to appear in random positions. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the sprite. Use randint to randomize the sprite’s x and y-positions, making sure that sprites do not appear too close to the edge of the screen. 


Click ▶ to see 5 sprites appear on screen in random positions!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new variable, then use it in the run condition of the for loop to create a random number of sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the randomNumber variable used in the for loop?

❓ How many times will the for loop run now?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The randomNumber variable is used in the run condition expression, which sets the condition that needs to be true, in order for the loop to run. The loop will continue to run while the counter variable is less than the value of the randomNumber variable. 

💡The for loop will run for the number of times indicated by the randomNumber variable, a random integer between 10 and 30.
steps.instructions:
Code a random number of sprites to appear when the project begins!


Declare a new variable above the for loop underneath // sprite set up. Type the keyword let and use randomNumber as the variable name. Use an assignment operator and randint to assign randomNumber a value between 10 and 30. 


Set the for loop’s run condition to the randomNumber variable. Inside the parentheses, replace 5 in the second expression by typing randomNumber. Now, the loop will run the number of times specified by the value of the randomNumber variable.


Click ▶ to see a random number of sprites appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you rename the counter variable, then update the initialization, run condition, and increment expressions so that the for loop begins at a number greater than 0 and decreases after each run?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many times will this for loop run? 

❓ What will happen to value of chances after each iteration?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The initialization expression assigns an initial value of 3 to the chances variable. The loop will run while the value of chances is greater than 0. Because the increment decreases the value of chances by 1 after each iteration, the loop, and the code inside of it, will run 3 times (3, 2, 1).

💡 Point out to the ninja that the decrement operator --works similarly to the subtraction assignment operator -=: it decreases the value of a variable, then assigns the variable the updated value. Unlike the subtraction assignment operator -=, the decrement operator -- always decreases the variable’s value by 1, since there is not a value on its right hand side.
steps.instructions:
Use another for loop to run a chunk of code multiple times, decreasing the counter variable each time the loop runs.


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath // user input. The counter i in a for loop is a variable, and can be renamed. Inside the parentheses, replace i in each of the 3 expressions with a new variable name: chances.


In the previous for loop, the loop began at 0 and counted up while the run condition expression was true. In this loop, update the 3 expressions so that the loop begins at a value greater than 0 and counts down. 


In the initialization expression, replace 0 with 3 to set the number of chances the user has to guess. In the run condition expression, replace < 5 with a greater than relational operator > and 0. In the increment expression, code the loop to decrease by 1 after each run by replacing ++ with --. The decrement operator -- subtracts 1 from the counter variable after each iteration of the loop. The code should look like:

for (let chances = 3; chances > 0; chances--) { } 

Now, the loop will begin counting at 3 and run as long as the counter is greater than 0, counting down by 1 through each iteration.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the loop counter variable to show the number of chances that remain?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the chances variable used in the showLongText code?

❓ What happens when the for loop runs?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The chances variable is used in the showLongText code to tell the user how many iterations are left in the loop. The pause delay and the guess screen allows the user to see each iteration of the loop. This value can be used to share information with the user.

💡 When the for loop runs, the project will pause for at least 1000 ms, then prompt the user for a number and tell them how many chances remain.
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to ask for user input and tell them how many chances they have left!


Add a delay between when the user sees the random number of sprites and when each guess screen appears. Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop under // user input. Update the parameter to pause the game for at least 1000 ms to give the user time to count the sprites on screen.


Underneath the pause code, use the keyword let to declare a new variable named guess. Type an assignment operator, then open Game and drag [ask for number (message)] to the right of it. In the message parameter, use concatenation to join a string and the value of chances, to tell how many chances remain. Use 2 as the answerLength parameter, so that the user can only submit a 2-digit number as their guess.


Click ▶ to see the project ask the user to guess how many sprites are on the screen and tell how many chances are left!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use equality and relational operators to check for 3 different conditions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you add 2 else if conditions to the conditional?

❓ What type of message should appear if the user’s guess was equal to the randomNumber? If it was greater than or less than the randomNumber?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their project to make sure that they’ve used the correct keywords, symbols, and syntax. If an error message appears, encourage the ninja to use it to identify where the problem is in their code. 

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Give the user feedback about their guess!


Open Logic and drag [if else] underneath the variable code, inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Turn else into an else if () condition, then add a second else if () { } condition to the bottom of the statement.


Inside the parentheses of the if condition, replace true with code that uses an equality operator == to check if the value of guess is equal to the value of randomNumber. Copy (Ctrl + C) the code inside the parentheses and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the parentheses of both else if conditions. Change the equality operator to a greater than relational operator > in one condition and a less than relational operator < in the other.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] into each of the 3 conditions. Update the string parameter so that a message tells the user whether their guess was correct, too high, or too low, depending on the value of guess. Update the layout parameters, too. 


Click ▶ to see the project tell the user how their guess compared to the actual number of sprites, each of the 3 times they guess!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you code 3 separate messages using showLongText to show, depending on if the guess variable is equal to, greater than, or less than the randomNumber variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition should be true in order for the game to end in a win? To end in a loss?

❓ Do the dialog box messages appear as intended?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the user’s guess is equal to the value of randomNumber, then the game should end in a win. If after 3 tries, the user’s guess still is not equal to the value of randomNumber, then the game should end in a loss.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their project to make sure that they’ve used the correct keywords, symbols, and syntax. If an error message appears, encourage the ninja to use it to identify where the problem is in their code. 

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Set the game to end in a win or a loss, depending on if the user guesses the correct answer. 


Open Game and drag 2 [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath // game end. Update the string parameter in the first showLongText to tell the user that they did not guess the correct number. In the second showLongText, use concatenation to join strings and the value of randomNumber to tell the user what the correct answer was.


Open Game and drag [game over (true)] underneath the showLongText code inside the if condition. Keep the parameter set to true, so that the game ends in a win if the user guesses correctly. Add another [game over (true)] underneath // game end and change the parameter to false, so that the game ends in a loss if the user guesses incorrectly after all 3 tries.


Click ▶ to see the game end in a win or a loss depending on how the user answers!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help players understand how the game is played? Did you add a pause between the directions so that the user has enough time to look at the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!


Open Scene and drag [set background color to (color)] underneath // game set up. Set a color parameter using a number 1-15.


Open Game and drag 2 [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath // user input, above the for loop. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow. Add a [pause (100) ms] in between the 2 dialog boxes, so that the user has enough time to look at the screen before guessing how many sprites there are.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Counting Sprites
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses for loops to give the user a set number of chances to guess the number of sprites on screen.

validationItems.text: Write a for loop and update its run condition expression so it runs a random number of times.
Inside the for loop, create a sprite set to a random position.

Write a for loop and update its initialization, run condition, and increment expressions so it begins counting at 3 and runs as long as the counter is greater than 0, counting down by 1 through each iteration.
Inside the chances for loop, create a variable and use the askForNumber function to assign it a value from the player. Use the value of chances in the message.
Use a series of if and else if statements to tell the player if their guess was correct, too high, or too low. If the guess is correct, end the game.
End the game if the player guesses correctly or if they run out of chances.
Add a background color and instructions for the player.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about for loops. Using for loops, you can code things to happen multiple times. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Getting Loopy
badges.description: Control how a loop runs using its 3 expressions in JavaScript.

badges.title: Here We Go Again
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts at zero and counts up using an increment operator.

badges.title: Where it Stops, Nobody Knows
badges.description: Write a for loop that runs a random number of times.

badges.title: Sugar, We’re Going Down
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts with a number larger than zero and counts down using a decrement operator.

badges.title: Double the Fun
badges.description: Nest a for loop inside another for loop.

badges.title: Memory Palace
badges.description: Save the game’s high score.

badges.title: Trophy Room
badges.description: Display the high score to the user.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Set a sprite’s z-position so it appears in the front of a scene.
